name: alex

status.note: Last release 11.0.1 in August 2023; the last commit, a README change, was in November 2024.

summary: A Node.js linter that flags gendered, ableist, condescending or profane wording in Markdown, MDX, HTML and plain text, and suggests neutral alternatives.
intro: alex catches “insensitive, inconsiderate writing”. Given `We’ve confirmed his identity` it suggests `their`; it flags `master` and `slave` and suggests `primary` and `replica`, flags condescending words such as `obviously`, gendered job titles and proverbs, ableist phrases and profanities. It skips words meant literally, such as a quoted `“he”`. The rules come from two plugins for retext, a natural-language processor, `retext-equality` and `retext-profanities`, and alex runs them through parsers for Markdown, MDX and HTML so it reads the prose, not the markup.

It runs as an npm CLI (`alex docs/`) or a JavaScript API. Each finding names its rule, so `.alexrc` files can `allow` or `deny` rules, `noBinary` decides whether pairs like “he or she” count, and `profanitySureness` sets how likely a word must be to be profane before it is reported. HTML comments such as `<!--alex ignore dad-mom-->` silence one paragraph. Community integrations cover Vim, VS Code, Sublime Text, GitHub Actions and Slack, and Vale ships the same rules as its `alex` package. The project has had no release since 11.0.1 in August 2023.
strengths: A focused rule set for inclusive language, each finding with a suggested replacement
Markdown, MDX and HTML aware, with per-paragraph ignore comments for deliberate wording
Easy to add to an existing JavaScript project’s test script and CI
limits: Word-list matching produces false positives (the README’s own example flags `pop` as a parent word), so most teams keep an allow list
Covers only inclusive language and profanity, not style, terminology or readability
No release since 2023 and little activity since; the Vale `alex` package is an alternative that runs in a broader prose linter
Needs Node.js, and the API is ESM-only since version 10

story: alex started from a tweet in July 2015 that raised the problem of inconsiderate wording; Titus Wormer (@wooorm), encouraged by Sindre Sorhus, built it on retext, a plugin-based natural-language processor from the unified collective that dates from 2014. The first commit was in August 2015 and 1.0.0 reached npm that September, followed by attention on Product Hunt and press coverage.

Later versions added MDX support (9.0, 2020) and moved to ES modules (10.0, 2021), while the word lists grew in `retext-equality` and `retext-profanities`. Releases stopped after 11.0.1 in August 2023.

choices.choice: Build on retext plugins instead of a standalone parser
choices.why: retext already turned natural language into a tree that plugins inspect, so the rules could live in reusable plugins (`retext-equality`, `retext-profanities`) and alex only had to wire up the inputs and output.
The README says alex assumes good intent; findings are warnings with alternatives, and comments or config can turn any rule off.
